Photograph: Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Trump promises new Iran talks as Tehran touts Hormuz shipping deal with Oman US president says he called off another US attack on Iran as part of a push for an agreement. Plus why Pokémon Go is still bring global joy 10 years on Martin Belam Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.36 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Donald Trump said talks with Iran would happen on Monday but declined to set a deadline for an agreement, after earlier saying he had called ⁠off an imminent attack. For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait of Hormuz, and it had no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one to any talks. On Saturday night, Trump claimed on social media that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal ⁠that would lead to “the immediate, complete and total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. He added that Tehran must “rapidly make a deal”. What has Iran said about the strait? The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baqaei, told state television on Sunday that a deal was close with Oman over a new route through the waterway. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview. RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak View image in fullscreen Robert F Kennedy Jr has for years amplified misinformation about vaccines. Photograph: Daniel Heuer/Reuters Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles , as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. How many measles cases has the US seen? His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289. Taken together, in the past two years there have been more measles infections in the US than in the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases was recorded in a single year was in 1991. Republican calls for Max Miller to resign from Congress after abuse allegations View image in fullscreen Max Miller has denied the allegations against him. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters The Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his former son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter Emily Moreno against the congressman. The senator’s statement came hours after Miller gave a live stream Sunday morning denying allegations of domestic and child abuse and insisting he would remain in the race for re-election. The public appearance came before Wednesday’s deadline to replace him on the ballot. “Just want to be clear: no court, no agency has ever substantiated any allegation of abuse against me. No criminal charge has ever been filed against me,” Miller said on the live stream. Family to sue after woman released from ICE custody froze to death View image in fullscreen Daphy Michel was found dead at a bus stop. Photograph: Michel family/AP The family of a Haitian immigrant who froze to death in early March at a bus shelter in Pittsburgh after she was dropped off in the city by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is poised to file a lawsuit this month against the US and “multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities”, the Guardian has learned. Daphy Michel, 31, had been in county jail for six months after a reported mental health crisis and street incident, and then was arrested by ICE before being released with an ankle monitor. In other news … View image in fullscreen More than 900 people are battling the Spokane Complex fires. Photograph: Tyler Vanwert via Reuters Eastern Washington fires have destroyed 600 structures and forced 60,000 people to evacuate , stretching the ability of federal and local agencies to fight the blazes. The chaos of a mass border crossing has given way to limbo for Moroccans on the streets of Ceuta , the Spanish colonial enclave in northern Africa. Marcy Kaptur is being treated ⁠for non-life-threatening injuries after a car crash in Toledo, ⁠Ohio, on Sunday, ⁠the ​Democratic US representative’s office said. The suspect in an Idaho restaurant shooting that killed three people died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound , police said. Pressure on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to step down has increased as members of Europe’s footballing authority Uefa prepare to oppose his re-election. Stat of the day: Spider-Man: Brand New Day makes debut to $927m box office View image in fullscreen Tom Holland and Marisa Tomei pose before the Spider-Man: Brand New Day premiere in London. Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/AP The Marvel Studios president, Kevin Feige, has hailed the movie’s “phenomenal” opening – the second biggest opening weekend in history – which followed a box office already buoyed up by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5. Building Power: How free childcare started winning US elections View image in fullscreen The Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP Sunny Patel reports for the Guardian’s Building Power series on Francesca Hong, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, who is part of a wave of democratic socialists finding traction with an old idea. Don’t miss this: ‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all View image in fullscreen The Pokémon Go character Quaxly in London. Photograph: Niantic/The Pokémon Company/Martin Belam I originally started playing Pokémon Go as a going out activity with my children. Ten years later, they have (mostly) put away childish things, but I still play it every day without fail. In this lovely piece , Sammy Gecsoyler speaks to devoted players who explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe. … or this: Hide the Pain Harold and Rubik’s Cube creator among social media’s picks for Hungarian president View image in fullscreen Péter Magyar, the Hungarian prime minister. Photograph: Robert Hegedus/MTI/AP Péter Magyar and his newly elected Tisza party asked the public to put forward names for the next president of Hungary, which is resetting its politics after years of being dominated by the rightwing populist Viktor Orbán. The suggestions have ranged from the sensible to the downright bizarre . Climate check: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’ – South Korea records its highest ever temperature View image in fullscreen Children play at a fountain to cool down during a heatwave warning in Seoul. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, at 42.5C, as authorities warned people to immediately stop all outdoor activities in affected areas. London’s Kew Gardens has gone without rain for a whole month for the first time in history, as Europe continues to battle a heatwave. Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens , killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified. Last Thing: ‘The greatest arms I’ve ever seen’: Matt Damon’s muscular female stunt double Devyn Dalton View image in fullscreen Devyn Dalton standing in for Matt Damon on a poster for The Odyssey. Photograph: Landmark Media/Alamy A 35-year-old stuntwoman is one of the great unsung heroes of Christopher Nolan’s new blockbuster The Odyssey – standing in for Matt Damon and displaying what the actor called “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”. Canadian Devyn Dalton was the Hollywood star’s stunt double in a pivotal scene. Olivia Bowden spoke to her . https://www.dw.com/en/yemen-houthis-take.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MOu4 The port city of Mokha lies near the crucial Bab el-Mandeb strait [FILE: August 10, 2026] Image: Al Joumhouriya TV/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement Yemen's Houthi militia captured the port city of Mokha (also spelled Mocha) on Thursday, sparking fears the country could return to civil war . The city lies around 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, an important waterway for shipping that divides the Red Sea from the Gulf of Aden. The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran , sending global oil prices skyrocketing. Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets. The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz. "The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying. Dhubab lies just south of Mokha. For a long time, Mokha had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government [FILE: September 2021] Image: Planet Labs Inc./AP Photo/picture alliance Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels intensifying efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline. The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022 . The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west. The internationally recognized government has its headquarters in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia. Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine. https://seenandheard-international.com/2.text: United States Haydn, Mahler: Cleveland Orchestra / Petr Popelka (conductor). Mandel Concert Hall at Severance Music Center, Cleveland, 30.10.2026. (MSJ) Petr Popelka conducts the Cleveland Orchestra © Aireonna McCall-Dubé/TCO Haydn – Symphony No.80 in D minor Mahler – Symphony No.5 in C-sharp minor Speculation about who is to become Franz Welser-Möst’s successor in Cleveland has been heating up. Czech conductor Petr Popelka made it clear in interviews with local media before his two weekends of concerts with the Cleveland Orchestra that he regards these performances as a job interview. So, how did he do? No one-word answer will suffice. Having heard Popelka as a guest three times, it is obvious that he thoroughly knows the scores he conducts. He has strong concepts and mostly delivers on them in performance. He is a master of the dramatic pause, and conducts quiet, intimate music with intensity. The problem that keeps returning in Popelka’s performances could be described as an excess of good taste. Simply put, he restrains everything marked above forte and seems unwilling to cut the music loose. Make no mistake, his Mahler Fifth was good except for that constant governing of the brass and percussion. But any performance of this work which makes Christoph von Dohnányi and Franz Welser-Möst’s Cleveland performances look freewheeling by comparison is too restrained. Excessive politeness was also an issue in the first work of the concert, Haydn’s Symphony No.80. One could argue that Mahler No.5 is a big enough work and doesn’t need a program mate, but one can’t complain about a chance to hear one of the less-familiar Haydn symphonies. No.80 matches with the Mahler inasmuch as it starts in the minor and ends in the major, but its world is very different, not least in the much smaller orchestration. It may well be one of the works influenced by Haydn’s theatrical work in the 1770s and 1780s for the entire first movement is a well-sprung setup gag: the opening music is highly dramatic although Popelka arguably understated it. After a tense pause, the composer completely undercuts the apparent seriousness with a flippant close of the exposition section. Popelka never rushed the pauses, giving the work its full comic timing so that it still worked delightfully. The Adagio movement was elegantly unfolded, though the following Menuetto was arguably a little ponderous. The Finale: Presto also felt a touch restrained for a composer who loved to tease both audience and players. All-in-all, it was a solid performance of rare repertory that would have been better if the conductor weren’t always erring on the side of caution. After intermission, the performance of the Mahler got off to an imperfect start with a wayward opening fanfare, but it is a notoriously naked start. These things happen. What is more important is that this blip didn’t prevent the orchestra from strongly establishing the symphony’s expressive world. Rhythms were subtly sprung so that the music’s tread was solemn but not heavy. Popelka showed insight when the second appearance of the lyrical subsidiary theme was more urgent than the first time. But the first disappointment came with the sudden acceleration marking the beginning of the development which wasn’t all that explosive in this performance. In his renditions (and in his Decca recording), Dohnányi demonstrated that the passage could be controlled in tempo but still burn. Popelka seemed more concerned with not hitting the passage too hard that early in the work. While long-term planning is good, the problem that emerged was one of Popelka restraining things over and over again at virtually every climax. Is this his absolute view of the work, or was he trying too hard to appeal to the vaunted Cleveland Orchestra poise? One hopes that the orchestra will never lose that inner coherency, but it is not a one-trick pony. They can blow the roof off when appropriate, and if it isn’t appropriate in Mahler, when is it? Mahler is the fellow who, when confronted with Niagara Falls, reportedly exclaimed, ‘At last, a true fortissimo!’ If he writes for a passage to be loud, take him at his word. It became even more of an issue in the second movement, the part that made the great German conductor Wilhelm Furtwängler swear off ever conducting Mahler’s Fifth because he couldn’t face the music’s ‘nihilistic’ ending. While it may not be true nihilism, the movement definitely tears apart its own attempts to rise up to brightness … or, at least, it should. Popelka, unfortunately, restrained any attempt by the brass or percussion to show strength, inhibiting what should be a hair-raising experience. Right in the middle of it, however, was a glowing passage performed to perfection: the slow recitative passage for the cellos. The performance suddenly snapped to emotional attention as the conductor encouraged the low strings to dig into a rich, burnished sound after a breathtakingly quiet start. In that kind of music, Popelka strikes gold. The third movement was better, as Popelka encouraged the players to spring rhythms, turning what can be a leaden ländler in some hands into a careening waltz for giants. Alternately playful, graceful and anxious, the movement unfolded with a fine balance of spaciousness and forward drive. Nathaniel Silberschlag played his solos standing at the head of the horn section, unlike in 2019 when Franz Welser-Möst had him come downstage to stand by the podium. The position made little difference for Silberschlag filled the hall radiantly. His solos and the pizzicato string interludes were redolent with emotion, although the closing of the movement was, again, kept on too tight a leash. Woodwind principals Joshua Smith (flute), Frank Rosenwein (oboe), Afendi Yusuf (clarinet) and John Clouser (bassoon) offered gleaming but characterful solos as well. The highlight of the concert came in the famous Adagietto where Popelka thrived on the music’s intimacy and encouraged the Cleveland strings and harp to play like their lives depended on it. It was magnetic, gorgeous and emotionally compelling, proving that Popelka can make glorious things happen in the right music. The following Rondo finale (played without pause, unlike the break between the first two movements) started at a good pace and gained momentum from there, with Popelka finally letting the orchestra loose in the closing pages which were negotiated with nimble flair. The audience response was highly enthusiastic. As job interviews go, it was fair, although not a clincher. Popelka will follow with Brahms’s German Requiem next week while fellow contender Santtu-Matias Rouvali comes to town soon with Richard Strauss’s Heldenleben . Local media thinks it is down to a battle between these two. We’ll see. Mark Sebastian Jordan 10 thoughts on “Popelka auditions for Cleveland with vivid quiet moments but a tight leash on peaks” Thanks so much for this thorough and thoughtful report, which I’ve been anticipating all weekend. While I’ve been living in Philadelphia for 38 years, I grew up in Cleveland and it’s still what I think an orchestra should sound like. Pity about the over-restraint, though if you had to deal with Yannick N-S regularly, that might be more welcome! I look forward to your report about Rouvali, whose work last year in Philadelphia I enjoyed. Reply That’s a fair enough point about YNS, but after twenty years of Dohnányi and twenty-five of Welser-Möst, I’m tired of restraint. There’s more to music than just reserve. What I’d like to see is a conductor who can maintain the orchestra’s poise, while letting them play powerfully more often. Tricky task, to be sure. I’m fascinated by Rouvali (who will be back soon). He can be amazing at times, then he’ll do something bizarre for no apparent reason. But he at least gets the idea of balancing the CO between poise and power. Reply If the orchestra sounds terrible, as Philadelphia does often under YNS, less restraint isn’t a virtue. I can imagine that 25 years of FWM might make one think otherwise! Lord knows I was done with YNS three years go, when he’d only completed 11 here. FWM was a regular here before he landed Cleveland, and he clearly wanted to be Sawallisch’s successor. But the PO was obsessed with Rattle, which of course never happened, and we wound up with Eschenbach, which was a disaster. Funny enough, the young FWM I heard in Philadelphia could be pretty intense at times. FWIW, late Sawallisch, when he became more emotional after his wife’s death, was the greatest sustained, ongoing musical experience of my life. Popelka is still relatively inexperienced, and I’d be very surprised he’d be able to start both an important opera house and a major orchestra successfully at the same time. Maybe go with Rouvali and make PP principal guest? Reply Thanks for your review! The Sunday afternoon concert felt the same as was described in this review. The Haydn was lifeless and the the Mahler was timid – very disappointing. I hope for better with the Brahms. Reply Thanks Mark for an excellent review as always! I attended Sunday’s ‘audition’ and came away less than impressed. The Mahler 5 was way too refined; the complete opposite of Klaus Mäkelä’s glorious Mahler 5 with TCO three years ago. The Haydn was the same; it just didn’t quite come to life. Your take on Rouvali is spot on! I am super excited to see him with Ein Heldenleben in a few weeks, especially after that nearly flawless Schubert 9 he led TCO last spring. Hoping a decision is made soon on the next Music Director. It is safe to say we are now in crunch time! I do not envy the decision makers, such an awesome task! Reply Who else is on the list being considered? Additionally, do you know who made the recommendations for the particular ones? Daniele Rustioni came twice to conduct here and he is fantastic. Is he on the list? Reply I wish I knew the answers to those questions. All I can do as a critic is to give my own perceptions and summarize what I hear elsewhere. The Cleveland media seems to think it’s down to Popelka versus Rouvali, but that too is just speculation. Rustioni received mixed reviews and isn’t considered a frontrunner by most commentators. If it were left up to me, I’d opt for Manacorda, though he’s not a high-profile choice. I think he’s a stronger interpreter than either Popelka or Rouvali, and he has been back a few times, but he’s not on this year’s schedule, which suggests he’s not being looked at any further. It could indeed be down to Popelka or Rouvali, but I wouldn’t rule out the possibility of a surprise candidate emerging late in the running. Only time will tell. Reply My sense from one state over (who can read cleveland.com on Apple News) is that the Cleveland media says what the orchestra administration tells it to. Moreover, this week it sent Adella subscribers (I am one) an email urging us to watch the next two streams, Popelka and Rouvali, in a way they haven’t done so before. Rustioni, fwiw, seems to have crept into a position in Philadelphia where he’ll be a candidate to succeed Yannick. Reply If negative reviews were a factor for the Cleveland Trustees and Management, the last three MDs wouldn’t have been appointed. The obvious choice is Rouvali. Cleveland has bypassed several candidates and they landed elsewhere. I’m not suggesting these would have been better choices, but Rouvali (and perhaps Rustioni) can generate a bit of audience enthusiasm that’s been so lacking in Cleveland particularly pre-COVID. Rouvali is not perfect, and as MS has noted, he tends to take long pauses. This is particularly evident in his Sibelius recordings, but perhaps as a Finn that’s his prerogative. However, he has had some success in Cleveland, is available and would probably be willing to take up residency in the Cleveland area. Despite his lack of opera experience, which has always been a major factor for Cleveland, he’s the leading contender. Not my personal top choice, but an improvement over the incumbent. Reply Thanks so much for your reply. I am stunned that Rustioni got a mediocre review. I find him to be a wonderful musician, and the orchestra sounded great under him. I live in Cleveland, and this year I only bought tickets for Stephen Hough in recital. Last year we went to concerts F W-M didn’t conduct. I find him a mediocre musician at best and I am at a loss understanding how or why he was retained here 24 seasons. My other gripe with the Cleveland Orchestra is that they keep inviting the same soloists like a revolving door (Ohlsson has been here 3 times in the last 2 years) or they bring NAMES rather than top artists. When a guest cancels, the audience is never given a reason why; you cannot return the tickets and get a refund either. You are forced to accept what they serve. Since Pittsburgh is close by, we have started going there instead. On the 29th we are going to hear my beloved Malofeev with Honeck!
